utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Pupovac. Yesterday when you started testifying you made a declaration to the effect that you would tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. I just want to remind you that you are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth today. Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pupovac, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before I continue with the examination, I would just like to briefly remind you to speak slowly for the benefit of the interpreters, and may we make pauses between my questions and your answers. Thank you. Yesterday, towards the end of the day, you mentioned a certain man called Miljanic, and somebody in an invalid chair told you about him, a civilian, a civilian whom you assisted. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that man Miljanic was? What was he doing there in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miljanic, according to what this other man told me, was the commander of a platoon fighting against the regular army of Yugoslavia, and he had the assignment of fighting with all available resources against the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you something else now. Did you follow these trials on television, the trials held here on television?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did follow some of the proceedings but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of hearing of a man who testified here with that name? Do you happen to remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't attend that particular trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When this civilian in the invalid's chair told you, in the wheelchair told you that Miljanic forbade the population, who were ethnic Croats, to withdraw from the village before the fighting, did he say why he banned that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, and in talking to him, the conclusion I arrived at was that, quite simply, they wanted to show the world that there were a lot of casualties, and in order to demonstrate that, they forfeited their own people, which is a horrendous thing to do for any nation in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you spoke about the civilians who were evacuated. Can you remind us -- or, rather, do you remember how many civilians from the village of Skabrnja you evacuated?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember -- or, rather, are you referring to the wounded and injured or civilians who were not wounded and injured?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for asking me that. I was thinking of the civilians, not the wounded and injured but the inhabitants of the village who were pulled out during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were over 150 people, men, women, children, who were pulled out of the combat. I don't mean pulling them out physically, pulling their bodies out, but withdrawing them from the combat activities, and they were transported to Benkovac where they were provided with food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice. In view of your last answer, does that mean, when you -- or, rather, if I say that there were any pregnant women, would that remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are asking a leading question, Mr. Milovancevic. You see, once you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the answer, Your Honour, I think that clears the situation up and I won't insist on the question. Yes, I do agree with you, Your Honour. That could have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was your attitude towards the wounded and towards the civilians? Did you differentiate at all between the people when you were working as a nurse on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a nurse, I cannot make any differences between -- treat people differently because they are all my own people from my own country, Yugoslavia, people who lived in the area. They were of a different religion, but I can't act differently towards anybody, and all the more so as I have relatives among the ethnic Croats myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Around the 18th of November, 1991, you said towards evening on that date that the fighting stopped. Where did you yourself stop in the village of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the centre of the village where the church is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to know the following: Did you have an opportunity of entering the houses to see whether there were any casualties? Did you do that, in fact, on the 18th and 19th of November? Did you go into the houses?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go into the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When, on that 18th of November, 1991, you stopped in the centre of the village, did you personally, and other soldiers, did they know or could they have known where the forces who were in Skabrnja were located, these soldiers that you were fighting against? What part of the village and were they in the village at all?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 18th or the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they still had the positions around the railway station. I'm referring to the Croatian paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the night between the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, was there any fighting, any shooting at all?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a quiet night. All you could hear was voices shouting out, "This isn't Serbia, you Chetniks. This is Croatian land," and various abuses of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the following day, on the 19th of November, 1991? You said that you spent the night in the centre of the village. What happened the following day?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following day we advanced along the road towards Nadin to Skabrnja, Nadin-Skabrnja, which was very important for lifting the siege, lifting the blockade at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought we are in Skabrnja. Now the following day, we are advancing along the road towards Nadin, to Skabrnja. I thought we are already in Skabrnja. Where are we going to now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there seems to be an imprecise interpretation there. I'll repeat that question and then she can give us her answer, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As you were saying, you were in the centre of the village. And the next day you set off along the road. Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We continued along that road and it's still part of Skabrnja. It's the area above the railway station of Ivkovici and then you reach the village of Nadin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, at least roughly, how far Nadin is from Skabrnja, the village of Nadin from the village of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one follows on into the other. They are connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you move along that road from Skabrnja to Nadin? Do you remember that? How long did it take you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we progressed very slowly. There were some sporadic shooting during the morning, but we were very cautious and wary so we moved slowly and there weren't any casualties in Nadin, and we passed through Nadin by 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that there was a little shooting. Who shot at whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Milovancevic. Your question had been how long it took them. To say they passed Nadin by 2.00 p.m. when we don't know when they left doesn't tell you how long it took. Can you establish that fact, please? At least she must tell you when they left Skabrnja to reach Nadin by 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I followed the witness's answer, but I'll ask the question again. I don't think that the interpretation was precise enough perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it this way: At what time the following day, on the 19th of November, 1991, did you set out from the centre of Skabrnja? What time was that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning at around 7.00 a.m. But we passed through Nadin by 1400 hours, 2.00 in the afternoon. That's what I said in my first answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. When you say 2.00 in the afternoon, 2.00 p.m., that's on the 19th of November, 1991. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that when you entered Nadin, and you explained to us that Skabrnja and Nadin are two neighbouring villages, that there was a little shooting. Who shot at whom?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian paramilitaries, what was left of them, shot at the members of the JNA, Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained to us that there weren't any casualties there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't. We had some wounded towards Nadinska Glava, which was mined when they withdrew. When I say "they," I mean the Croatian paramilitary forces. There were anti-aircraft mines that had been laid, trip mines, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Anti-tank mines, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In respect of the village of Nadin, where is this place that you mentioned Nadinska Glava or Nadinska Greda. Is that the same thing?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called Nadinska Glava. That's what it was called the whole time, and I think that in the present state of Croatia the name has remained the same. Nadinska Glava is an elevation which is a very important feature in the area from which you would be able to control all the roads running from Benkovac to Ravni Kotari, that is the Benkovac-Biljane Gornje-Smiljcic road and Islam-Kasic road. And then the Benkovac-Biljane Donje road, because it passes above Nadinska Glava. It's about 100 metres as the crow flies. Then the Benkovac Biograd road. And the large Zadar airport, you can control the whole of that area from that vantage point. Yes. You asked me about the roads leading to the Zadar airport; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that from Nadinska Glava you can control all the roads and including the Zadar airport, how can you control them and who did this controlling? Who controlled them?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the war operations you know how this was controlled. They could prevent any passage along those roads, anybody from passing, civilians and soldiers alike, if you were up at Ravni Kotari, that elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And how would you do that? What means would you use, what resources?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I was able to see, and I did see this at the end, they were well armed. They had mortars, 60- and 82- and 120-millimetre mortars. They had hand-held grenades. They had the zolja type of weapon, hand-held grenade, and some artillery pieces as well. I don't know what they were called. Of long-range weapons anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your answers you mentioned the basic positions held in Skabrnja, the Glava [indiscernible], Nadinska Kosa, Nadinska Glava. Were there any other positions or were they the only fortified positions from when they opened fire while you were in Skabrnja on the 18th and 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they opened fire from other positions as well. Zemunik Donji is located between Skabrnja and the airport. A place called Prkos below Skabrnja and Galovac, another place. So from three axes, they were able to target Skabrnja from these three axes apart from the elevation which is in Skabrnja itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you reached Nadinska Glavica and took up your positions there, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the army was withdrawing to its reserve positions. They went back to barracks like any other army, any other soldiers returning back to barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go after that operation?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to the TO commander and returned to Benkovac, of course. Zoran Lakic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- or, rather, do you know what happened to the civilians who were evacuated from Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those civilians were first of all taken to Benkovac, those of them who were not injured and wounded. Anybody who was injured and wounded were taken to a clinic to be given medical assistance. The civilians who arrived in Benkovac to the barracks there were fed and they were also put up in the children's nursery school. And they expressed the desire to cross over to Zadar because they had relatives there. However, through some friends who were working there, they asked that the Croatian authorities receive them in Zadar. This was a hot line, because you weren't able to communicate in the normal way with Zadar, but Zadar refused to allow them to do that. Since they insisted, and since there was a cease-fire anyway, in the area of Pristeg, Ceranje Gornje, that is a location which is south towards Biokovo [as interpreted] underneath Benkovac, the road to Sibenik turns left. Anyway, they took the people to that crossroads, the crossroads, the junction, between Pristeg and Ceranje Gornje. Ceranje Gornje is a Serb village; Pristonje [as interpreted] is a Croatian village. And they had to pass that area on foot. I think that their own people gave up on them. That's my opinion. And they didn't want to take them in, but they had to go and cross over to Croatian territory on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, all this happened in November 1991, how long were you when you resided in your home town and in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 4th of August, 1995, until the Croatian fascist action of Storm, which drove me from my home, and now I'm currently residing in Serbia. So until the 4th of August 1995, in early morning hours, I left my home town and my home village and my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could it be said that you left voluntarily, that you wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. The first question got by and the answer started before I could object. But there is nothing in the 65 ter summary about, you know, when she left her home or anything after 1991, as far as I can tell, so I would object to more evidence on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept this. I just wanted to make a connection between the place of residence that the witness informed us about at the beginning of her statement, and the place which she left. Thank you, Your Honours. Defence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not 1991, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Your Honours, Defence has thus concluded the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume you're saying that you are withdrawing that last question against which there was an objection. Thank you very much, if that is the case. Any cross-examination, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. If I could have just a moment to send my list to the Defence, please. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mrs. Pupovac, my name is Mr. Black. I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case, and I'm going to ask you questions for a while now. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Drmanic and my -- Pupovac is my maiden name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Most of my questions are going to be specifically about the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, about the operation in Skabrnja, but there are a couple other things I'd like to ask you about. For example, yesterday you said -- and this was at transcript 59 to 60 for Your Honours and Defence counsel. You said that the 1990 elections resulted in the HDZ and Ustasha party taking power, and throughout your testimony you've referred often to Ustashas. My question to you is this: You considered the HDZ and the newly elected Croatian authorities to be Ustashas; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the authorities and their attitude towards the Serbs and that kicked a sovereign people from their constitution in 1990 and turned them into a minority in a country where they used not to be a minority, that authority has to be labelled an Ustasha authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So I guess the answer to my question was yes.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Ustasha authorities even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you still hold that view now?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still hold, as long as my people do not have the right to truth, that they did not leave their homes voluntarily, that they were expelled by the Ustasha governments, as long as my people do not have the right to their property and as long as the so-called homeland war is not characterised --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for what it is because of the actions -- please let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you can finish if you focus on my questions. There is a procedure here and it's I ask you questions and then you need to answer my questions. So please try to focus on them and don't go on talking about other things. You're kind of getting involved as long as this, as long as that. Focus on my questions, okay, please?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I focused on your question, and in that question, to that question, there is only one answer. Let's remember Medak pocket on the 20th January, the largest holiday for the Serb people. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, you may not. You really -- there is -- you really need to focus on my questions. After I get done asking my questions, then counsel for Mr. Martic will get a chance to ask you questions again, and if there is things that weren't clarified or that I didn't ask you about and he thinks that need to be clarified, he can ask you more questions. Just so you understand that. But you need to really focus on my questions and just try to answer them, okay? Do you understand that? And I would add, you know, the purpose of us being here is not to argue about these things. My job is to put questions to you and your job is to answer them the best you can, so we don't have to try to argue about it. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only answer that I can give was the one that I gave you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on to another question. You referred in your testimony several times to the chequer-board symbol. Am I correct that you considered that red-and-white chequer-board symbol to be an Ustasha symbol, not merely a Croat symbol but an Ustasha symbol; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, under the chequer-board symbol, my mother from 1941 to 1945, during the World War II, lost her child, while she was handcuffed by the Ustashas and the Germans and the Ustashas wore that chequer-board symbol. And now 16 years she hasn't seen her other second child. That's me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we please understand each other. What the lawyer has been telling you is that you must focus on his questions and answer his questions only. Please, it's very important. He hasn't asked you about your mother. He just asked you about the chequer-board colours. Concentrate on what you are being asked. We understand you may have emotional attachments to these things because of what you -- according to you has happened to you and your mother. Try to restrain yourself and keep to the question. Okay? That way we'll finish quicker. And you will go home earlier. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One other thing that you mentioned in your testimony, you talked about "redarstvenici," and I hope I'm pronouncing that close to correctly. Now, you describe the "redarstvenici" as HDZ paramilitaries, and you said how they wore Ustasha emblems. These people that you've described in those terms, that was just -- those were Croatian policemen, correct, that's who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Yugoslavia still existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But even when Yugoslavia existed, Croatia had a Ministry of the Interior, right? There was such a thing as Croatian policemen, even during the SFRY, right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But the symbols were different, not the chequer-board symbols, but the five-pointed red star.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me focus on this word "redarstvenici." I just wanted to know if the people that you described as HDZ paramilitaries and Ustasha, the people you were talking about were members of the Croatian MUP, correct, Croatian policemen?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were of the HDZ, policemen of the HDZ, because the proper authorities had not been established. They were part, political party policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you consider the SAO Krajina police to be paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krajina, I don't know which period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm talking about from the -- well, actually from August 1990, all through 1991, mostly in 1991 when the SAO Krajina was in existence and they had their own secretary and later Ministry of the Interior and they had their own police. Now, did you consider those SAO Krajina police to be paramilitaries in the way that you've described the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Because they wore the symbols of the state of Yugoslavia that was still in existence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, actually, the SAO Krajina police had their own patch that said "Milicija Krajina" on it, didn't they? So they didn't actually wear the symbols of the old police.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They still hadn't put any other symbol on those insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So even in 1991, let's say in November of 1991, you weren't aware of the Milicija Krajina patch worn by the SAO Krajina police? You're saying that didn't exist then?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you forgot that I was a nurse, not a policewoman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right. I didn't actually forget that. Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Black, I must admit I thought she was admitting that they did wear the Krajina Milicija, but saying other than that there was no other emblem, so I don't know if you could clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, you may be right. I didn't notice the word "other" in that answer, so perhaps that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It may just be my understanding it could be clarified further for better understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I accept what you say. I had missed the word "other" in her answer. Let me put just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, just so that I'm clear, so you accept that the -- and I know you were a nurse but you accept that the SAO Krajina police wore the Milicija Krajina patch, and you say other than that, they still wore the old insignia? Is that -- could you explain it to me because as you can tell I didn't really understand why you were saying that the SAO Krajina police were not paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you put an answer that suits you in your question, but I cannot answer your question as it was put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me put my question to you again and see if you can answer it this way. To you -- in your mind, why were the Croatian police in 1991 paramilitaries and yet the SAO Krajina police in 1991, at the same time, you don't consider them paramilitaries? Just please explain that to me and I'll move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because no fascist symbol was put on the uniforms by the SAO Krajina policemen as opposed to the others, those others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about another thing you said yesterday. You said that the HDZ wanted to break up Yugoslavia, "With the help of foreign states that wanted that." And I just wonder if you could explain that a little bit more. Which foreign states did you mean and what were their goals, according to you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Germany and the USA, countries that recognised the break-up of Yugoslavia, followed by others, affected through the secession of Slovenia and Croatia through their attacks against the JNA, Slovenia and Croatia started the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Because yesterday it seemed like you were talking about 1990. But are you saying that you're talking about events that happened later, with the recognition of the independence of Croatia and Slovenia in 199 -- well, their declaration in 1991 and later their recognition in the international community? Is that what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, taking into account German aspirations during World War II and later, the importation of arms, the arrival to the front line of volunteers from these countries, importation of arms from those countries, would it not be tantamount to a break-up of a sovereign country? Sir, this was the most beautiful country on earth. Very beautiful, with lots of diversity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, would you say that you have a tendency to exaggerate things? Or would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well let me ask you about one example. You testified yesterday about the horrible murder of the Stegnjaja couple. First of all, that happened in September of 1991, not in 1990, as you suggested, right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot really remember all those dates spanning five years. But that's no the reason for you to accuse me of exaggerating, because the murder of a single bird would be too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you accept that that happened in 1991, rather than 1990? Or you just don't remember?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me move on to the actual facts of what happened because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But wait a minute. What's your answer now? First of all you say you cannot be expected to remember all those dates. Now you say you do not accept that it was 1991. Now you tell us, when was it, according to your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to say that it was -- occurred before any other armed conflict. There still was no armed conflict at the time. There were no attacks, direct attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is no question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And still one could travel to Zadar and back from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you? There was no mention of armed conflict in the question. I'm just asking you a question: When did it take place? Was it 1990 or was it in 1991? Just be specific and let's get over this point and get to the next point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot really specify the date. What I know is that there -- this was a heinous murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you then accept that it could have been in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, on this same event, isn't it the fact that it happened as follows: Those people were -- weren't taken off of a bus but, rather, they got off of the bus one day because it didn't stop at their usual stop and so they had to walk across a field to get back to their village, and they were apparently killed in that field and their bodies were discovered some two months later. The man had been decapitated, as you said, but his head was never found, and the wife had been beaten to death. Isn't that what actually happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were taken off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you have asked several questions, if you can break them up. Walking in the field, man decapitated, woman beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I was trying not to spend too much time on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But she has answered only one of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think there is a way we could do it if we could use a document. If we could at ERN 01445726, please. If we could see that on the screens in front of us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, you can see this has been translated into what's there in front of you in your language. This is a document actually compiled by the FRY, by the Yugoslav authorities. And you can see there it refers -- gives this description of the killing of the Stegnjajas in September of 1991. If we could scroll down just a little bit, perhaps the witness can just read that to herself and we'll read it silently to ourselves. And, Witness, when you've had a chance to finish it tell me if you accept that as the correct description of what happened on this occasion. Ma'am, when you've finished reading it, please let me know and I'll continue with my questions, but please take your time. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So having seen this, do you still insist that these people were pulled off of a bus by paramilitaries and they were both decapitated and they switched the heads, or is it the case that you exaggerated the already gruesome facts of this murder?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I exaggerated. I don't know who compiled this report either. And this is based on the story of a woman -- as told by a woman who was on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted as evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Can we just establish where this document comes from, who compiled it, when, where? Its provenance, whose document is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't want to testify about this, but my information is that this is an FRY government document compiled in response to a United Nations Security Council document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is that written, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It can be deduced if you -- if I had more specific knowledge from the heading, Your Honour, at the top, the YU/SC 78092. I'm relying on what I was told by an analyst. This is -- that's as far as I can take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there nothing on the B/C/S copy, original, to give us an indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think actually the English copy is the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: English copy is the original. Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic? I'm told, Mr. Milovancevic, that that YU/SC and those numbers give you the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this document, it says Stegnjajici. The persons killed did not have that surname. The surname in fact was Stegnjaja, according to the testimony of the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the second point is this. All I can do is to believe my learned friend, take him at his word. I'm sure he received the information that he conveyed to us. But I would like to see what document it was that is being presented to the Court, if it is going to be tendered. From what I can see before me, nothing can be deduced, absolutely nothing. It doesn't say who compiled it, who it was addressed to, when it was compiled, or the purpose it was written for, whether it was signed, unsigned, sent, not sent. It tells us absolutely nothing, Your Honour. So what I want to say is that this is not a proper document. We cannot accept it. The Defence cannot accept it as a document of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is noted but --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Exhibit number will be 994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, before you proceed Mr. Black, there is a question I wish to ask of the witness that I'm not quite certain about. Mrs. Pupovac, at page 19, lines 20 to 22, you said you were not exaggerating and that this is based on a story of a woman as told by a woman on a bus. Which one of the stories are you saying, yours -- what you have said or what is in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here Branko Stegnjajic. That's not the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What have you said -- all right, let me find the specific portion because I have it written down but let me read back to you verbatim. Now, you were -- it was suggested to you that you exaggerated the already gruesome facts of this murder, and your answer was thus: I don't think I exaggerated. I don't know who compiled this report either. And this is based on the story of a woman as told by a woman who was on the bus. When you say "this" what are you referring to, what was in the document that you looked at or your own story? Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the story that I recounted, but this is the story about another man called Stegnjajic. The other man's name was Stegnjaja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One other thing: As far as you're aware, did your incident take place on the 13th of September, 1991, allegedly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know. About the incident you asked me about, I don't know. Stegnjajic I don't know anybody like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The incident that you have told us about, that you are saying that we should rely on as correct, did it take place in September of 1991 or when did it take place as known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think it was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Was it in September, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact date or anything like that, but the whole of Krajina knows about that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Where was the bus coming from and where was it on its way to? Where was the bus coming from and where was it on its way to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Benkovac-Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would that be the same as Zadar-Posedarje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What has Posedarje got to do with Islam Grcki? They had nothing to do with that. When they were going to Benkovac to Zadar, Posedarje is to the east from Islam Grcki. It's got nothing to do with that. The person who compiled this report, well, I don't know who that was or what their purpose was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And where would the Nova Bistrica agricultural estate be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea. I've never heard of that agricultural estate. Never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What about Islam Grcki?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Islam Grcki is a large Serb village in Ravni Kotari, which is located next to another big Serbian village by the name of Kasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So none of those places figured in your report that you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. And to begin with, this family has nothing to do with Posedarje. And I've never heard of Nova Bistrica or that agricultural estate there. And the surname doesn't correspond to the other one either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, then, the following: It isn't said that the family has something to do with Posedarje, is it? It was just a mentioning of the bus, Zadar-Posedarje. And you said that this makes no sense to read it this way. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I didn't express myself in the best way. If people are going from Benkovac to Zadar, they have no way of going to Zadar via Posedarje. There was a road at Islam Latinski going that way, and from Biljane to Zadar, but as to this here, nothing seems to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What road has a bus connection in connection with this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Benkovac-Kasic-Islam Grcki-Islam Latinski, and then the road goes down to Zadar through Murvic to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the names be repeated, please? Sorry, they are not written here so we are not able to check them out in the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to repeat? Kasic, Benkovac-Kasic. Do you wish me to repeat the villages that come before Kasic or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe we can try to understand how this description should be read or can be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Starting from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Starting from Zadar, apparently. It is said in this document that this couple was working in Zadar at a newspaper. Nacional List. And they were on their way back from work on that day, by the Zadar-Posedarje bus, as usual. Do you know this bus? Have you used this bus line already in your life? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. That bus for Posedarje I have no need to use it if I'm going to Benkovac, because that would take me to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, no. It's okay. So this -- if someone would live in Islam Grcki, what way would this person then use if going by bus from Zadar? Give me every reasonable possibility. And if you don't exactly know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know I would go through Murica, Zeleni Hrast, and then enter Islam Latinski and Islam Grcki, and then the bus for Islam Grcki was the only one going to Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean, "the bus for Islam Grcki was the only one going to Benkovac"? We don't need to go to Benkovac, do we, in this hypothetical case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it's the bus route that was used. Zadar-Islam Grcki-Benkovac was the bus route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And this would not go by Posedarje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We will go into this matter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Posedarje is on the way to Maslenica as you go to Zagreb, in the direction of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt, but I think the important thing here is whether or not these people that she was talking about were from Islam Grcki or not, and if she could answer that that might be enough for us to know whether we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So in your eyes these people you reported about, where were they from? The couple you called Stegnjajic, Stegnjaja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Stegnjaja couple were from Islam Grcki. And I've never heard of Stegnjajics at Islam Grcki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So can you spell that once more, what the family name in your eyes was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] S-t-e-g-n-j-a-j-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the first name of the man and his wife, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know them. I don't know their first names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we can go any further in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In fact, I'm about to broach a new subject. Perhaps -- it's a couple minutes before our regularly scheduled break but it would be a convenient time, unless Your Honours want me to press on for the next two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt your cross-examination, Mr. Black, but there is this little housekeeping matter that needs attention. It's pretty urgent. The Trial Chamber will now render its decision on the second Defence motion for protective measures for Witness MM-105 which was filed on the 31st of August, 2006, whereby the Defence seeks the assignment of face and voice distortion to Witness MM-105. The Prosecution has informed the Trial Chamber in its response on the 30th of October, 2006, that it would not object to the granting of voice and face distortion should they be requested. The Trial Chamber notes the arguments of the Defence and finds that the Defence has established that there exists an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family. The Trial Chamber further finds that the requested protective measures are appropriate for the protection of the witness. The requested protective measures for Witness MM-105 are therefore granted. The registrar is ordered to enable voice and image distortion during the witness's testimony. Thank you very much. The witness may be brought into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, before you proceed on to your next area of cross-examination with the witness, I'd like to have a look at that last document for just two seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. In fact, over the break we found one more document that I hope could clear this up about the day at least, so I'll show that to her. The last document received, Exhibit number 994, so if we could see that on the screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, would you like to put some questions before I resume on this document or shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to have a look at it. Thank you. I do not think any questions will arise out of it. Thank you very much. That's sufficient. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mrs. Drmanic. I just have one more document to show you on the last topic that we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So with the assistance of the usher, I could provide the witness a copy and also copies to the Bench. Your Honours, this is something we just pulled off the net. It's in B/C/S. It's quite simple, but we will provide a translation as soon as we can get one through the system. And I provided a copy of this to Defence counsel during the break of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, are you familiar with the Veritas organisation? Have you heard of that before?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to look at this document which, two-page printouts from the Veritas web site, and you'll see there it refers to Branko Stegnjaja and Anka Stegnjaja, and it says that they were killed on the 13th of September, 1991, in Islam Grcki. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this document and the one that you showed are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's right. This is a different document now, but it's on the same subject. And so I just wanted to ask you, before you weren't sure about the date, but seeing this document, do you agree with me now that the Stegnjaja couple that you talked about, they were killed in 1991, not in 1990? Do you agree with that, having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree because I was told that they were killed then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: When were you told that, please, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was told to me a long time ago, while we were still in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No more precise answer possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war period. I was told during the war period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean between 1990 and 1995. I met that woman who told me what she experienced and that she experienced all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure we could take it any further. Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit 995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm turning now to a different subject. You testified yesterday that you saw dead civilians when you were in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991. But then you also suggested it was difficult to distinguish civilians from combatants, et cetera, and just so we are clear, according to you, were crimes committed by the attacking forces in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you phrased this question wrongly. No forces were attacking Skabrnja. The forces of the Yugoslav People's Army were attacked by the paramilitary formations and forces at Skabrnja. When it comes to your question concerning the civilians, I did see, of course, killed people in the streets in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to this issue of attack or who attacked whom. But you've said now that you saw killed people in the streets in Skabrnja. But my question for you is were -- were innocent civilians intentionally killed in Skabrnja, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have to reiterate, not in the streets but in the street, the single street of Skabrnja, which the army took. The street is a very wide term. And for somebody to be intentionally killed by the Yugoslav People's Army, that I believe was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So regardless of streets or where it happened, you're saying that as far as you know, no civilians were intentionally killed in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw, there were people killed by shells or bullets, people who were caught in the cross-fire. Many of them have been pulled out by us and they were later exchanged. I believe that I was quite clear while I was testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you see them being killed, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir. I could not see that -- I could not see when anybody was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you know they were killed in cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because a group of people were passing between the positions held by the Croatian forces. They were in the basements, together with the combatants. All able-bodied men, as far as could be seen, were armed whether wearing a uniform or in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you see people passing between the positions held by the Croatian forces maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People that we saved are those that we managed to save from the fire-fight. Those who were later exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not my question. Did you see those people passing between positions held by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatian forces, the Croatian paramilitary forces, were together with them in the basements and they opened fire from basements, from Razovljeva Glava. From all houses, they opened fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we'll deal with basements. Just answer my question. You said because a group of people were passing between the positions held by the Croatian forces. I'm asking you did you see them passing between the positions held by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did you see people in basements together with the combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, basements were the places where fire was opened from and civilians emerged from these basements and the basements were the places where fire was opened from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you see this fire being opened from the basements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of course. Because I was there. I did not go back with my team. I wanted to stay there for me to be able to provide first aid, because there were opened -- they opened fire at the van marked with a red cross and the people who were wearing the Red Cross arm band.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, did you then see the cross-fire? Did you see them being hit in cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not lift my head, because I was targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you didn't see anybody being hit in cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were hit at the time when fire was opened from both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, my question is very simple. You did not see people being hit in cross-fire, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I pulled out the wounded people that I could pull out. I couldn't -- I did not see who was hit from which side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not -- that's not my question. You did not see people being hit in cross-fire, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, we heard evidence in this trial that on 18th November, 1991, you intervened to save the life of a young boy named Marin who was about to be killed by a soldier. And according to the account that we heard, you were with two other people, apparently nurses, and when the soldiers wanted to kill this boy, you said to him something like, "Don't kill him. We've had enough of such things." That happened, didn't it? Do you remember something like that happening? Or do you say that it never happened?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you can remember no incident where you saved the life of some young boy?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I -- I never saved anybody's life in this way. I did save some people, some wounded people, several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about a -- I think appears to be a different episode. If we could look at Exhibit 116 on our screens, please, on e-court? And, ma'am, you'll see that this is an Official Note. It's compiled by a security officer of the JNA 9th Corps, and it's dated the 8th of March, 1992. You can see there in the first paragraph, that according to the document, it deals with the killing of civilians in Skabrnja and Nadin on the 18th and 19th of 1991 [sic]. You can see there in the first bullet point, I just want to ask you about this, you can see it says: "All the collected data shows that the killings were committed by members of the Benkovac Territorial Defence Staff special units or units that fought under their command. These were volunteers from Serbia and Opacic's group composed of combatants from the area." My question for you, ma'am, is: Can you confirm this or deny it? Do you have any information about what's stated in that first bullet-pointed paragraph there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, there were no volunteers, only our Territorial Defence and the Yugoslav People's Army. When it comes to Opacic's group, I know Opacic. I know him well, very well. He used to be a policeman in Yugoslavia while it existed. I can state with full responsibility that he wasn't in Skabrnja. Opacic was more involved with politicians, providing protection to police -- politicians. I can state with full responsibility that Opacic was not even in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you -- I guess you confirm that members of the Territorial Defence were in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I confirm that they were there, but I'm not confirming that they committed the crime as alleged here. This report was compiled in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Setting aside for the moment whether they committed crimes, can you -- you confirm, don't you, that they were there and they participated in the fighting at least, putting aside the issue of crimes? I'm talking about the TO.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the TO were under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Whoever's command they were under, you can confirm, can't you, that they were present in Skabrnja engaged in the fighting. That's the only thing I'm getting at right now, just that they were there and that they were involved in the fighting. It's not a question from the document. It's a question about what you know, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But it says here there were volunteers in the TO. There were no volunteers within the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see from this, it says that there were volunteers. Volunteers were not part of the Territorial Defence. Somebody invented this out of thin air, and this report was compiled, I don't know for whom, and on the basis of which data.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I'll just answer that question so you can see this was compiled for the JNA, the 9th Corps command, and it says that it's based on talks with personal and official contacts and having examined the unit's combat documentation. You see that in the first paragraph. So just so you know who this is for and on what basis. But, please, can you just answer my question? I don't think it's a difficult one. Can you confirm that in fact members of the Territorial Defence participated in the fighting in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army, not autonomously but under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army, and this was compiled by an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. What was his intention with this? Maybe to clear his own name. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, please don't speculate about things you don't know, and you don't need to ask questions. I'll take care of asking the questions. But I think it's almost clear from your answer but you keep kind of giving these explanations. Yes, yes, members of the Territorial Defence participated in the fighting in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991; correct? Just answer that clearly and then I'll move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't separate the TO from the JNA, when they were under a single command, sir. You're forcing me to say something that does not stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I'm not asking you anything about command. I don't care about command for this question. I just want to know if people who were members of the TO, they belonged to the TO, and they fought in the action in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991. Whether under the JNA command or whoever's command, I'm not interested in that right now. But it's true that TO members fought there; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I'm able to read, if we eliminate one word from the context that would -- it says they were volunteers. Now, there were no volunteers in the TO, whereas it says here that it was the volunteers who --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excuse me, and I apologise for interrupting, but you really need to focus on the question. I'm not asking you about the document. I'm asking about you and what you know, because you said that you yourself were in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991. And I'm just asking the very simple question: Isn't it true that members of the TO participated in the fighting on that day? Please answer that. I think you can answer it yes or no. And I'll move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this kind of document, as you've been showing me, and the answer that you wish to get from me is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, forget about the document for a second. Don't think at all about the document. And don't, you know, try to think about the answer that I'm trying to get. I just want you to tell the truth. Isn't it true that on the 18th of November, 1991, members of the Territorial Defence participated in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did take part, under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we could scroll down, please, to the bottom -- actually that's perfect right there. Ma'am, you can see that the -- what's now the first visible bullet point, it's actually the third bullet point on the document, and if you look at the second sentence, it says -- follow along with me. It says: "Members of the Serbian volunteer unit apparently interrogated a captured member of the ZNG who was beaten in the process. This was witnessed by three nurses in a blue van from the Benkovac Territorial Defence Staff. And one of the nurses stood up to Vucicevic. "Vucicevic demanded that the member of the ZNG shows him where the mortar is, then he led him away, and as soon as they disappeared behind the house a burst of fire was heard and Vucicevic returned alone." Ma'am, you testified yesterday that you were there with two other woman nurses and that you moved around Skabrnja in a blue van. This must be referring to you; isn't that right? What's stated in this document refers to you and the other nurses?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was referring to us, but I didn't know Vucicevic nor did I see Vucicevic in Skabrnja, nor did I see this killing, the killing of this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, if you don't know Vucicevic, how do you know if you saw him in Skabrnja? Maybe you saw him and you didn't know it was Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I told you that I didn't see this incident take place at all. I didn't see this episode. I didn't see this member of the Zenga who had been arrested, that they beat him, and that three nurses were there in a blue van. I saw none of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You agree with me, though, that there weren't any other nurses in any other blue van in Skabrnja on the 18th of November; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you don't remember anything like this. You can't -- this incident does not ring a bell with you at all?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think we are done with that document. Thank you. It can be taken off the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I get back to that? Witness, can you explain us, has anybody interviewed you among the people who might have set up this report? So that must have been, then, between November 1991 and March 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the reports and everything that I saw I conveyed to Mr. Lakic. That was my duty. And he was the TO commander of Benkovac. What I saw -- now, I really don't know anything about this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you by any chance know a Lieutenant Commander Simo Rosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Major Milivoje Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging by the surname I know what village he was from. But no, I don't know the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Maybe just look at the -- you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, you've suggested yesterday and again today that every able-bodied man in Skabrnja was a combatant on the 18th of November, 1991. I just want to show you a couple of photographs on this issue about combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see Exhibit 270 on the screen, please? And if we could actually turn to page 7835, the ERN -- that's the end ERN number there, photographs F 2 and F 2A.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, ma'am, these are photographs that purport to be -- have been taken by the Benkovac SUP on or before the 21st of November, 1991. It's a little hard to distinguish, but there are two people there, two dead people. You said that you didn't go off the roads, but I'm just checking, did you see these people when were you in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't know what I saw. I pulled out the wounded and the injured. If anybody was wounded or injured, we pulled them out, administered first aid and transported them. I know that there were three or four elderly persons, two or three men, I know that I managed to pull out a child who had been wounded in the leg. I think the child's name was Ivica. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You talked about that a little bit. I was just wondering do you remember seeing these people? If you don't, that's fine. But do you remember seeing these people?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't know whether these were the people. I saw dead people. But on the basis of this photograph, I can't say. I didn't know the people for me to be able to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that there were people who were dead. And this isn't on the road, sir. This is a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're correct that this is not on the road. According to eye-witnesses, these older people were taken out of a basement where they were hiding with other civilians including children, and then these people were -- these older people were each shot in the head by Serb fighters. Did you hear anything about such an incident?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot claim, sir, that these acts were perpetrated by Serb fighters. That would be biased, because there were no Serb fighters at the time. The Yugoslav People's Army, sir, is what there was at the time, not Serb combatants or fighters. When there were Muslims and Siptars and Serbs and Hungarians and what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm just repeating to you what the evidence was in this case. I'm not qualifying people one way or another, but that's what was said so that's why I put it to you, okay? My question is did you hear anything about such an incident as I've described to you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that if that account is true, that these people were civilians, right, not combatants, these people we see in front of us?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you just showed me some people in front of a house. How can I know under what circumstances these people were killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand your definition of civilian, I guess. And so if what I've described to you is true, that these older people were taken out of a basement under the control of soldiers and shot in the head from a close range, would you agree with me that they were civilians and not combatants?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing is true, and that is that there was shooting coming from cellars. So together with civilians, there were their side's fighters. Now, how they were killed, I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you can't answer this question, you can say so. But if what I've told you is accurate, that these people were taken out of a cellar where there were no fighters, just civilians, and in any case, if they were under the control of the soldiers and they were shot in the head from close range, you'd agree with me that they weren't fighters, they were civilians, right? Or do you resist even that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer a question like that because there was shooting coming from cellars. I can't say who was killed in what way and you can't really see anything or deduce anything from these photographs. All you can see is dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a couple other photographs. These are the page with the ERN ending 7849. Ma'am, take a close look there. Do these people look like combatants to you, or are they civilians, as far as you can tell from the photograph? We can scroll down to see maybe the last photograph as well.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians. But it is also a fact that this is a stamp, our stamp, and that you can see that they didn't wish to hide anything but that everything was done above board and professionally and that nobody wanted to conceal anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Having seen these photographs, would you now agree with me that civilians were intentionally killed in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991? Or are you still unable to agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm still unable to agree that they were intentionally killed, if I didn't see them actually being intentionally killed and the circumstances under which they were killed, and whether the wounds were from a grenade or from a bullet or whatever. How can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. We are done with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Whose stamp are you saying it is when you say "it's our stamp"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The stamp of the interior affairs department. I can see that it's the police that conducted the on-site investigation. We can see it says "Benkovac" and it says "public security Benkovac." So I assume that there was no attempt at concealing anything. Had an intentional genocide been perpetrated, they might have just buried the bodies without anybody knowing anything about it. And as far as I can see, if that it is the proper stamp, and if it is the Ministry of the Interior, as it says here, that's what I can see. There was no attempt to conceal anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Madam, you're using the word "genocide." Did I hear that correctly? If yes, then what do you mean by that? When are you using that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wasn't thinking about genocide, genocide over these people. Nobody reasonable would have perpetrated such an act. All I wanted to say by saying that is that if you have the Ministry of the Interior here, if that's what it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you repeat that question, then, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean by "genocide" if you used the word as you did in your answer, which made me ask that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Genocide in my view is the destruction of a people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, I take it this is just pure speculation on your part about whether there was a cover-up or there wasn't a cover-up. You're just guessing based on seeing the Benkovac SUP stamp on these photographs, right? Just so that we are clear about that.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's why you shouldn't have shown me documents that I have nothing to do with. I'm just giving you my own opinion based on what you've shown me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you don't actually know whether there was an investigation or trials or anything that flowed from these apparent crimes in Skabrnja, do you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think now we are done with that document. Ma'am, many of the victims who were killed in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991, were autopsied a few days later. According to those autopsies, 23 people were found to have been killed by gun-shot wounds. Now, you were there. Is that consistent with the kind of wounds that you saw on that day? Did you see a large number of people with gun-shot wounds?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say how many people were killed or how many casualties there were. I can't really give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was not about the numbers. The question was about gun wounds. Did you see people with gun wounds, gun-shot wounds amongst the people that you rescued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were wounds caused by firearms and grenades, at least as far as I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
