utterances.text: I understand when you say that you can't give a precise answer to how many people were killed or how many casualties were there. Can you give me an estimate of how many civilians were killed in Skabrnja on the 18th and 19th of November? Can you give an approximation?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a couple of specific cases. Stana Vickovic was born in 1936. The evidence shows that on the morning of 18 November, 1991, she was taken from a basement along with other civilians and shot in the head. She was one of the women that we saw in the photograph. Did you see any civilians who had been shot in the head specifically?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was not looking who got shot in the head or who was targeting whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said yesterday, ma'am, that you were giving these people whatever first aid you could give before you transported them to a physician who was going to look into detail -- into the detail of their medical condition. Isn't that what you testified about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. I spoke about people who were wounded. I was helped by the soldiers, by saying whether there were wounded people there or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said -- listen to what my question is: Didn't you say yesterday that the people that you found on the scene, you tried to give them whatever nursing care you could give, as much as you could do, and as much as you knew, and then you transported them to be attended to by a doctor. Did you not say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. But on the road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if you have said so, surely, to be able to give assistance, you've got to look at the injury. Isn't it so? You attend to the injuries when you give assistance, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But these pictures that were shown to me they were inside houses. I wasn't in houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, forget about the pictures, please. Listen to my questions. When you gave assistance to these people in the form of whatever nursing care you could, you did so by attending to their injuries, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would dress the wound before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To dress the wound you've got to know where the wound is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, then the question simply is: In the wounds that you dressed, did you see any wound to the head? Did you see any injury to the head of anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We don't have to struggle this much to get an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we see Exhibit 344 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mrs. Drmanic, you worked as a nurse. This is an autopsy report for Stana Vickovic and you can see there in the first line she was 55 years old and, according to this anyhow, she was killed in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991. If you look down in that first paragraph about the external findings on the body, about the fourth sentence there, it says: "There are two gun-shot wounds, one to the head and one to the lower right leg." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please, all the way to the bottom, I guess. Perfect. You see there, in the -- it's the top paragraph, the last sentence of the top visible paragraph, it says: "The wound was inflicted at close range." Do you see that? This is on page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the top of the page. Ma'am, this is consistent, isn't it, with the eye-witness evidence that she died from a gun-shot wound from close range, that she was shot in the head from close range, right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What have I got to do with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- you're a nurse, right? Have you ever seen an autopsy report before?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm -- well, if there is a particular reason, tell us and -- but I think otherwise you have to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an objection. In response to the Bench's question whether the witness saw on the ground or tended to wounds of people having head wounds, the witness answered no. The witness is not a medical expert to be able to answer these questions. In cross-examination, she said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you objecting to, Mr. Milovancevic? I'm trying to follow what you are saying here to understand what is it you are objecting to. Are you objecting to the questions that were asked by the Bench some minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I'm pointing out the fact that the witness in response to the Bench's question stated that she never saw a head wound out on the ground and that she could not say anything about that. She said, why are you showing me documents because I don't know anything about it because I never saw head wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: She's not being asked about any wounds that she saw. She is being asked about this document and the evidence that was tendered to say that the person was shot at close range. And she is just being asked if that evidence, together with the post-mortem report, are those two consistent? She is not being asked about anything that she saw on the ground. Is the post-mortem report consistent with a shot at close range? That's the question. She is a nurse. She has told us she's a nurse. She doesn't have to be a medical expert to have seen a post-mortem report before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, I understand what you're saying, but in this sense, I object. How could this witness answer such a question? Only an expert witness, a medical expert, could provide this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you need me to repeat the question or do you remember what the question was?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the question. I see that this was signed by a pathologist specialist. I'm not a pathologist. I really cannot answer such questions to give my assessment. If you're going to provoke me by your facial expressions, I'm quite ready for that as well. But, sir, I cannot answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Ma'am, please, you have to show respect to counsel. Whatever you're used to in your jurisdiction, then you have to forget it. You're not allowed to engage in repartee with counsel. Please respect him. The question that he has asked in the course of his duties, then you're duty here is to respond to him. He's asking you, have you ever seen a post-mortem report before, a very, very simple question to respond to and answer, and you have that knowledge, and please give it to the Trial Chamber. And, in future, please do not disrespect counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You have to be careful how you give your evidence and how you respond. Because it's part of the Defence case. Don't go beyond the line. I'm sorry, Judge, please, I realise that you wanted to say something. But, you know, madam, I have held back because I think you have been breaching the rules for sometime. You just have to learn that his duty is to ask you whatever question he chooses within the bounds of the laws of evidence, and we three will stop him when he goes outside. We will determine, not you. So please do proceed. And do the best that you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just add one point? That disrespecting counsel is tantamount to disrespecting this Court also. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, the first question, simple question: Have you seen autopsy reports before?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're able to follow along with what I showed you, and the reason I ask you is simply this: You've contended that there weren't intentionally killings of civilians in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991, but based on this autopsy report it would seem that this, Stana Vickovic must have been killed intentionally, correct, because she was shot in the head from a close range. Do you agree with me that that suggests that it was an intentional killing?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So give me the alternative explanation of why a 55-year-old woman would be shot in the head from close range and it would not be intentional.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that and I cannot provide any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you imagine any justification for shooting a 55-year-old civilian woman in the head from close range during combat?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you any explanation. I don't want to discuss this -- these documents. I have got nothing to do with these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, can I ask you a question? Do you want to testify in this matter? You have been brought here by the Defence to come and testify. If you don't want to testify, tell us you don't want to testify any further. We will find out from counsel what he wants to do with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I cannot testify on the basis of what I was shown. I did not see that. I cannot testify to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, do you want to -- do you still want to testify in this case or don't you want to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does -- what does that mean? What do you mean by yes? I didn't ask you -- I'm asking you do you want to testify or not? I want to know what do you say yes to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to testify about what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, fine. Then if you don't know a thing, you just say, "I don't know." You don't go into argument with counsel. Now if you want to testify, ma'am, the Judge has just told you a couple of minutes ago that your job here is to answer questions that are put to you, and if any question is put to you that is not proper, it is for these people sitting here to say to counsel, "That question is not proper." For as long as these people are quiet, yours is just one thing: To answer. Okay? Now, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, we have been discussing now intentional killings of civilians I want to ask you about something related but slightly different. Did you see or did you hear anything about fighters, combatants, who were intentionally mistreated or killed after they were captured by the attacking forces?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. We have another autopsy report. I won't ask you to look at it but let me just put its contents to you. It talks about a man by the name of Ante Razun, who I believe was in his 30s, and according to the autopsy report he was tortured before being shot in the head from point-blank range, and then he was mutilated, his left ear was severed from his head. First of all, did you ever hear about anything like that, any incidents like that at all?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. I heard about an incident of that kind but I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. What did you hear about an incident of that kind?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard that there was a man without an ear, but I don't know who perpetrated that neither. A young soldier told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, did you hear stories about someone with a bag of human ears or someone going to a restaurant, for example, and putting a human ear in a dirty glass? Did you hear about any kind of stories like that about ears?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Before I move on, would you agree with me that even if this man was a combatant, that such brutality is unjustifiable and that his torture and execution was a criminal act, even if he were a combatant?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me now take your attention to a different subject, so I'm leaving the 18th of November, 1991, for a few minutes. I want to ask you about some things that happened before that. You mentioned loyalty oaths yesterday. Let me ask you: By July and August of 1990, the Serb authorities in Knin were rebelling against the Croatian authorities; correct? They were rejecting the authority of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, I believe that the Croatian authorities -- authorities of the Croatian republic, a unit within the federal Yugoslavia, wanted to change the then valid symbols, the symbols valid in the then country. I remember that, and I remember that there was a rebellion about that, because until 1992 the valid symbols were five-pointed star and not a chequer-board, because the Croatian flag, the one -- the unit of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was red, white, and blue with a five-pointed star, and they put the chequer-board on the red, white, and blue fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, is it possible that these loyalty oaths which you talked about were simply a clumsy response to the Serb rebellion as Croats became afraid of what was happening in Krajina? Is that a possible explanation for why there may have been loyalty oaths?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why, but what I do know is that after those loyalty oaths, the people were dismissed, they were intimidated, and that they had to leave their companies in order to avoid being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's also true, isn't it, that there were some Croats who were forced to sign loyalty oaths or be dismissed from their jobs in the SAO Krajina. Isn't that also true?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you don't know whether that happened or not? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: From August 1990 onwards, Serbs in the Krajina were illegally arming themselves; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sure. Isn't it correct that from August 1990 onwards, Serbs in the Krajina were illegally arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know about incidents also from August of 1990 and really onwards, where Serbs blocked rail traffic, blew up kiosks, damaged private shops owned by Croats, all of this in an effort to create a situation of chaos? Were you aware of such incidents in the latter part of 1990?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my town, nothing like that happened. Not a single Croatian house was blown up. And looking at my village, because it has a mixed population, after our departure, when we were expelled from Krajina, all the Croatian houses remained standing, intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that says a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me keep you focused on 1990. What about other places, other towns like Knin or Benkovac? Did you ever hear about these kind of incidents in other towns in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't hear anything about that from your friends or neighbours or see anything in the paper or on TV?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that all the -- and I think today as well -- that all the roads between Benkovac and the Zemunik airport were blocked. I take it you were referring to the fall of 1991. Is that the time-period that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from 1990 onwards, you couldn't go to Zadar. The road wasn't open, and afterwards, the army withdrew from the airport. So there were no planes down there at that time or any equipment at the airport. And those soldiers who stayed on, they weren't able to -- supplies weren't able to reach them along the normal route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let's focus on the fall of 1991. At that time, the JNA was actively using the Zemunik airport. Flights were departing from the Zemunik airport. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during that period, when this happened, you couldn't go along any road. They were not passable. And you had to go through orchards, woods, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll ask you about roads in a minute, but my question was about the Zemunik airport. Isn't it right that in the fall of 1991 the JNA was using the airport? In fact, there were flights departing from the Zemunik airport in that period.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With regard to roads, isn't it correct that the JNA continued to travel from Benkovac and to Zemunik by going through Smiljcic? You can go the road up to Smiljcic? Isn't it true that the JNA continued to use that route in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the Zadar airport is located between the Croatian village of Zemunik Donji and Skabrnja, which is above Zemunik Gornji. The road passing from the airport towards Benkovac is the road through Donji Zemunik, which arrives at Tromilje, which is the junction. It's the crossroad between Zemunik Gornji and Skabrnja. One road leads to Biljane Donje, Benkovac, and the other branch of the road from Tromilje goes to Smiljcic, towards Benkovac, which means that the army, the soldiers, could certainly not have passed along that way, along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you deny that the JNA was able to reach the airport from Benkovac by going through Smiljcic? You say that absolutely did not happen.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to pass that way because the Croatian village Zemunik Donji -- you would have to pass through the Croatian village of Zemunik Donji if you took that route, because there are two roads which merge as a crossroads and that crossroads is called Tromilje. And one branch of the road goes towards Biljane Donje, and the other towards Smiljcici. And then you turn off towards Biljane through Bastica and the orchard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. That's plenty of detail. I think you've answered my question. You testified about an operation at Nadin in September of 1991, I think you said on the 30th of September, which you described as an attempt to enter Nadin peacefully. My first question on this topic: This wasn't some kind of peace mission, was it? This was an operation where the JNA and whoever else was with them arrived with tanks and armed soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every army has the task of defending the territory of its country. So the territory of Nadin and Nadinska Glava was the territory of the Republic of Croatia, a federal unit within the composition of Yugoslavia. The fact is that the army did not fire a single bullet before they, the Croats, shot at the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And everything was mined --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, but just on that point that you just mentioned, you say that the Croatian forces opened fire first, but even if that's as you say, it was only after the JNA and the TO came at them with tanks and armed soldiers, right? No one from Nadin went looking for the JNA. It was the opposite. The JNA came to Nadin.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the Yugoslav People's Army is an army. It is the army of the Serbs, the Croats, and the Slovenes, and the Macedonians, and the Montenegrins. That's what it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But I don't think that answers my question. I'm not interested in whose army was. The fact is the JNA and the TO went to Nadin, armed and with tanks, and that was how the conflict, the fighting there started, right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But sir, the road running from Benkovac to Biljane Donje and Zemunik airport passes exactly above Nadin, and it is controlled from Nadinska Glava. You can control it very well from that vantage point. And it can also be controlled from the village down below because it's so near the road. That you can certainly control it, which means that this wasn't safe passage for the soldiers, or the civilians either from Benkovac for that matter, towards Zemunik airport and the other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for all that narration that you told us. Will you please answer the question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Now you must listen to the question and answer that question. Don't formulate your own question and then answer it because then you forget the question that's put to you. The question is: The fact is that the JNA and the TO went to Nadin, armed with tanks, and that was how the conflict started; is that correct? Now, you should be able to say yes, it's correct; no, it's not correct. I don't want any further discussion from you beyond those two, one of those two. Is it correct or is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer that with a yes or a no. It's a complex question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's complex about the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's complex because before that, the Yugoslav People's Army was attacked, before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about what happened before. The question is the JNA and the TO went to Nadin armed with tanks and that's how the conflict there started. In Nadin, the conflict in Nadin. It started because the JNA went to Nadin armed with tanks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not enter Nadin. They were in Devici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... said they went there and that's how the conflict started. Is that how the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. You refuse to answer the question. We will make a note of that. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, what role did the TO, the Territorial Defence, play in this operation at the end of September, I think you said it was? Was the TO directly involved in fighting in that operation?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took part together with the JNA, under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I believe you said that the date of this operation was the 30th of September, 1991. Is it possible that it could have been closer to the 2nd of October? Are you sure about the dates or might it have been one or two days later; do you know?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we are at the time for our regular break and it's a convenient moment for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take an adjournment and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to our time allocation, Mr. Black, you've got one hour left with this witness to round off everything, depending on how much longer you think you will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it had been my hope to finish today, but the way things have gone, we've gotten side-tracked on a couple of things. I think it might be very close for me to finish at the end of the day today. I would say that this is an important witness who was actually at one of our crime scenes as opposed to we've had a lot of testimony about politics and other things. I think this is a very important witness. I will certainly go as quickly as I can, but I would ask that I at least have the rest of the day and perhaps a few minutes in the morning if necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's see how far you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'll certainly bear that in mind and move as quickly as I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept what my learned colleague has just said. We, too, consider this to be an important witness, and we have nothing against the request made by the Prosecutor. I'd like that to be understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ma'am, we were just discussing fighting at the end of September or perhaps at the beginning of October 1991. Just very quickly, there was also fighting actually in Polaca, which is about 10 kilometres away. There was fighting in May 1991; correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't really give any answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know that Nadin, the village of Nadin, was shelled in September of 1991? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Zadar being shelled between the 30th of September and the 7th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know that in early -- excuse me, early October 1991 after the fighting which we discussed before the break, most of the villagers of Skabrnja were evacuated to the islands and they only returned after the cease-fire agreement which was reached around the 9th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The reason I ask you all these questions is because isn't it the case that Skabrnja didn't set up its village guard for offensive purposes but rather to defend itself because of all the fighting that was going on in the area and the various aggressions by the JNA and other Serb forces during 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any aggressions, so I can't answer that really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, do you agree with me that the village guard in Skabrnja, the forces in Skabrnja, they were primarily defensive, not offensive? They were there to protect the village of Skabrnja and the village of Nadin; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who would defend a village from its own army of the existing state?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please don't -- try not to answer in rhetorical questions. Do I take it that you disagree with me that it was defensive, or do you agree with me that it was defensive?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Before I move on to ask you some specific questions about the attack on the 18th of November, let me put something to you for your comment, and just try to listen to this question carefully. I suggest to you that the attack on Skabrnja was an example of provocations by the Serb side, and by that I mean the JNA, the TO, and the police, provocations against the Croat village with shelling or other small-scale aggressions until the Croat village responded by arming or other resistance and then the Serb side used that response as an excuse to launch a full-scale assault, destroy the village and expel the inhabitants? Isn't that really what happened in Skabrnja in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not a military expert for me to be able to give you an assessment of the situation. I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you some questions that hopefully you'll be able to answer. First of all, you will agree with me that certainly in November, the operation on the 18th of November, 1991, against Skabrnja, that was an offensive operation, an attack; correct? It wasn't a defensive operation by the JNA but an offensive operation.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an offensive operation because the JNA was attacked first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But just like in September, the Croats from Skabrnja and Nadin didn't go looking. They didn't go out and take the fight to the JNA. The JNA and the TO forces and the police came to Nadin and Skabrnja; correct? They brought the fight to the village.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you're mixing up these things. The police didn't enter Skabrnja and it wasn't in Skabrnja. It was the Territorial Defence within the composition of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So you deny that members of the police, whether it be a group of police or individual members of the police, were present during the fighting in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no policemen in Skabrnja at all. The Territorial Defence within the frameworks of the Yugoslav People's Army of the state that it still existed which was Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say there were no policemen in Skabrnja at all, there were police involved in the operation; correct? You concede that much, don't you? Involved in the planning and in the execution of that operation.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not an officer of any kind, and I didn't see who planned the action, but I didn't see any policemen in Skabrnja. I know that there was the Territorial Defence there and the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you explained to us earlier that -- about, you know, that you were focused on medical aid and things like that. Is it fair to say that you saw what you saw and you say you didn't see any policemen but you can't actually rule out definitively the participation of some policemen in the fighting in Skabrnja, right? You can't say for certain that that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, because at the starting point there wasn't a single policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But after the starting point, once the fighting actually started, you can't -- you weren't able to see every soldier and all the activity and the fighting throughout the whole village during the fighting; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in Skabrnja, you could only enter Skabrnja by a single road, and since in the rear of the soldiers, to the rear of the soldiers, I was there and I could see the road and I could see whether a policeman had entered or not, and I claim with full responsibility that there was not a single policeman in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you claim that you saw every single person who took part from the -- on the attacking side in the fighting in Skabrnja, despite all the other duties which you've discussed to us, about pulling people out and crawling through the bushes to save wounded people, you're telling us that you could see every fighter who participated?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, from the starting point, when you set out, there was not a single policeman that moved in. We could see who was coming and going because you had to take the road. For them to advance, they would have to have passed by us, passed by the medical corps, rather, the nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And are you saying that it was impossible, that anyone would have entered Skabrnja from other directions other than through Ambar, that no one could have come in without you seeing them?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't enter because everything was mined through the forest so you couldn't take the forest route. You would use Zemunik Gornji, that parts of the road, that's a Croatian village, where there was no resistance, and nobody -- there were no fatalities either, and in Skabrnja there was a lot of resistance, and nobody went off the road because they would have been shot at from Zemunik Donji and Prkos and Galovac and they would have been like clay pigeons 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So I understand you, according to you, no one could have gotten into Skabrnja without coming through that one road and going by and through the JNA and the TO; correct? No one could have gotten through without the JNA and the TO knowing about it, and you seeing them?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Yugoslav side, no. Now, when it comes to the Croatian side, they could have got support from Prkos, Galovac and Zemunik because that part of the village was free, so they could have got reinforcements from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Just one more question on this and then I'll move on to a slightly -- to another question. You mentioned Goran Opacic, and you said categorically that he was not in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991. But you actually, in fact, you can't rule out him being there at some point. You may not have seen him, but you can't categorically rule out his presence, can you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Goran Opacic was not in Skabrnja, and I say that with full responsibility. Because Goran was dealing with security, the security and safety of individuals, politicians in Krajina. He was an active-duty policeman in Zadar, and they imposed the chequer-board emblem there and he rose up in rebellion in Zadar against that. He stood up and came out against it at a policemen's meeting; I know that. And then he left Zadar and arrived in Benkovac and provided security for politicians. He liked to talk a lot, brag a lot, but I do know that he provided security for politicians. And I say with full responsibility once again that he was not in Skabrnja on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned that he liked to brag a lot. But you know that Goran Opacic received awards for his bravery and his valour, both from the RSK police and from the Serbian police. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So that it's clear, I'm not sure, in the fall of 1991, Goran Opacic was a member of the Benkovac police; correct? Is that what you're saying? Or are you saying something different when you talk about him with politicians?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a member of the police force but I know that he provided security for political figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a member of the TO at some stage?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me move on to something slightly different. You referred to the death of JNA officer Stefanovic and you told -- you described how you arrived at the scene shortly after he was killed and you evacuated his body out of Skabrnja. Again, for clarity, you didn't actually see him killed; correct? You arrived after he was already dead.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you talked about one other JNA soldier who was killed in the same incident. Those were the only two JNA soldiers who lost their lives on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, in Skabrnja; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let's accept for the sake of argument that Stefanovic spoke on the megaphone in the way you described. At the very most, what he was offering the villagers of Skabrnja was sort of a last chance to surrender before the Serbs took over the town by force, right? That's the most that you could interpret out of what you say Stefanovic was saying in the morning.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the man meant. How could -- everybody has their own opinion. But the goal of the action was to lift the blockade of that road going towards the airport and I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Wasn't the goal of the operation all along really to take over the village and drive out its inhabitants? Wasn't that really always the goal?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, if the goal were sort of peaceful, as you've suggested, why were so many crimes committed against the villagers, not just on the 18th and the 19th of November, 1991, but crimes were committed up through February of 1992 against villagers in Skabrnja. Doesn't that indicate that the goal was really to drive the villagers out and to take over the village?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know how they got killed. What I do know is that there were civilians together with their soldiers. Therefore, army opened fire at each basement that they received fire from, not knowing who opened the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You've explained that. Let me move on to something else. You testified that Croatian forces in Skabrnja received artillery support from nearby villages, and you even said that it was Croatian artillery support that was destroying houses there. What leads to you believe that it was Croatian artillery that was destroying houses and not Serb artillery or JNA artillery?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, JNA artillery did not act. There were some tanks. It would be too close. Croats shelled our positions in Skabrnja and they were shelling their own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you say that it was somehow too close for the JNA to use artillery but the Croats went ahead and shelled their own village? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they shelled the village because we were in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The JNA also shelled Skabrnja on that day, didn't it? They used artillery, in addition to the tank fire -- the tank shelling.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no artillery preparation, and no shells were falling on Skabrnja before that. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So at 7.30 in the morning, for instance, you didn't see or hear any JNA artillery against Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified that there was gun-fire coming from the bell-tower of the church in Skabrnja. That's simply not true, is it? And you're just saying that to justify the damage to that church. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true, sir, that they opened fire from the bell-tower and this is why the church was targeted. The bell-tower was so high that you could see from the bell-tower where you can fire. I do not want to anybody. I'm here because of the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you do confirm that the church was targeted by the JNA forces, JNA and TO, although you say that it was because there was fire coming from there, right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fire was opened from the bell-tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you present when one of the tanks tried to actually drive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. The question was: So you do confirm that the church was targeted by the JNA forces, the JNA and the TO, although you say that it was because there was fire coming from there, right? The answer is: Yes, fire was opened from the bell-tower. The question that is being put is whether it was targeted, and that was not answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had interpreted the first yes as an affirmative, but let me put it to the witness again just so that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, just to go back to that last question. You do confirm that the church was targeted; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The church was not fired at as a Christian temple but what was fired at was the position, the nest that was in the bell-tower of the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But -- okay. You've given your explanation but fire was opened at the bell-tower, just so that we are -- at the church so that we are clear; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate, church as a Christian facility, was not targeted. What was targeted were the position of the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is not the question. The question is it was fired at, wasn't it? For whatever reason it was fired at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was -- there were firing at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Black, you asked about the tower being -- having been a target. And then you said the church. Was the tower separate from the church or was it one and the same building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bell-tower is right beside the church. On the church, part of the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So they are part of the same building. The bell-tower is one part the of the church building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I don't know if it is but it was at that time, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Correct, exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the time the bell-tower was part of the church building, right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you present when one of the tanks tried to actually drive into the church?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you see or hear anything about members of the attacking force entering the church, firing their weapons in the church, breaking things and attacking the altar of the church?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I did not enter any building in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't see any such thing happening at the church?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see because I wasn't in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that JNA soldiers didn't come off the road during the fighting, and you talked about how you yourself didn't leave the road. First of all, when you said that, did you include TO members? You're saying that no one, JNA or TO, left the road?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to the JNA and the TO because they were under single command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be practically impossible to take control of a village like Skabrnja without leaving the road? What about the fighters in the yards and buildings beside the road? Were they just left there to continue firing on the attacking troops, or how was it that they fought this battle without leaving the road?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fight was conducted exclusively from the road, and the free passage to evacuate the population was opened towards Zemunik Donji, Galovci and Prkos. The goal of the action was not to destroy the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you saying that people -- that the soldiers didn't leave the road because you know that crimes were committed at the houses and in the yards and pulling people from the cellars and you want to distance the soldiers from those crimes? Is that why you're saying that no one left the road?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that crimes were committed in basements. I'm not claiming anything and I'm not defending anything. I'm saying what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You also said and you've said several times that combatants and civilians were mingling together in the cellars of houses and you couldn't tell who was a civilian and who wasn't. My first question is you just said that you didn't leave the road. How do you know that civilians and combatants were mingling together in the cellars of houses?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because fire was opened at me, among other people, from those basements while I was providing first aid. And many of those civilians were evacuated towards Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But how do you know, even accepting for the moment that fire was opened at -- from cellars, how do you know that in those cellars there were civilians as well as combatants? How do you know that they were mingled and there weren't just some buildings where there were combatants and other buildings where there were civilians?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People came back to the starting point from those basements who told that they were in the basements, and the basements were the places where fire was opened at the JNA from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But those people didn't say that they were in basements with fighters, right? You don't actually know if there were cellars or basements where there were both fighters and civilians. You may assume that but you don't actually know it, do you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not assume. From those basements, civilians emerged and set out towards Krncetina. Now I don't know what was the name of the starting point in the direction of Ambar. I don't know who remained in the basements. They came there to the starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you never saw civilians coming out of a basement where you know that there were also combatants there, right? You never actually saw civilians and combatants together in a basement. That's just something that you've sort of assumed happened, but you didn't see it, did you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't assume. I saw from one basement ten people emerging. They set out towards Krncetina Novi. The military was directing them there, and that basement was where fire came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you changing your story as we go along so that it kind of gets better and better? Are you changing it to meet my questions? To fit with my questions?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to prettify anything. In this case, you cannot prettify anything because people were dead there. Nothing beautiful came out of it when you have war, when people lose their lives and the lives of their beloved ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I agree with you that we don't want to prettify what happened there. As I've said to you, there is evidence that civilians were taken out of basements where there were no combatants, just civilians, taken out under the control of the soldiers and murdered. Now, would you agree with me that if that happened there could be no justification for that, that that would be criminal, that those people didn't die accidentally or in the cross-fire or things like that? If people were in fact -- civilians taken out of basements and executed, that's a crime.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it were so, of course it would be a crime. But I cannot state it was a crime because I did not see one being committed. Of course, it would be a crime to kill somebody, anybody, and to deprive themselves of the right to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You claimed at the end of the day yesterday that you received some information from a villager in a wheelchair. In fact, this was one of the first questions today that Defence counsel asked you about. This was a person who you were evacuating, who was under your control and in a sense sort of at your mercy at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why at my mercy? Me who helped him, who fed him there? Why at my mercy?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I take it this person, and correct me if I'm wrong, but that person was extremely frightened under the circumstances when you talked to him, if indeed you did talk to him, right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't frightened. He led such a nice conversation with me. Maybe he felt secure. Maybe he was happy that he chanced upon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So when he was evacuated from the fighting in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991, he wasn't afraid, in fact he was happy? He was having a nice conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He led a very nice conversation with me. It was a spontaneous conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You claim that a person named Miljanic did not allow civilians to be pulled out of the village. But in fact, many civilians did flee the village, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many civilians fled. I know what he told me. The story was that a certain Miljanic would not allow civilians to withdraw, to leave them as a shield for the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You've already explained that. Just because we are short of time I don't want you to rehash your evidence. Those that did not flee on the 18th of November, 1991, it wasn't because someone told them not to, it was because this was absolutely no warning before this attack. People didn't have time to get away, that's why people -- the ones who didn't flee, the reason they didn't flee is because there was no time to flee. They just hid. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, whoever wanted to save their lives and who was allowed to withdraw, there was ample room for them to withdraw safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So is it really your evidence, as you just said here a moment ago and you said yesterday, that this person Miljanic intentionally sacrificed the villagers of Skabrnja? Is that what you're saying, that he used them as shields for the military or in order to gain sympathy?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Aren't you just trying to justify the crimes that were committed in Skabrnja by pushing that blame on to someone else, whether it be Miljanic or the Croatian side in general? Aren't you just trying to justify what happened there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not justifying any crime. What happened is horrible. Even if one person were wounded it would be difficult. I do not justify his actions, if he did that because of that purpose, for some other interest to sacrifice their own people. I would never sacrifice anybody or for them to be killed because of some other interests in that way. I did not say that. The person in the wheelchair said that. He allegedly -- stated that he allegedly was a policeman before he was retired, and he was in the wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a different topic now. After the attack on the 18th and the 19th of November, 1991, some civilians remained in Skabrnja; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you accept that after that time, and up until about February 1992, more than 20 people were killed in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know that people --

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know there were people killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And who as far as you know was responsible for those killings, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you give us any approximation of about how many people were killed? Do you know even approximately?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. So I cannot give you a figure. I would be mistaken whichever figure I may give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. Thank you. There has been evidence in this case that in December of 1991 TO members were killing elderly people in Skabrnja. Did you ever hear about anything like that in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which TO members? Which TO?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe the Benkovac TO, Your Honour, the SAO Krajina TO, not the Croatian TO, if that's the import.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified that when the troops moved on to Nadin on the 19th of November, 1991, there was -- well, I think you said sporadic shooting but not much resistance. Do you know or did you hear anything about nine civilians being killed in Nadin on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that then. I heard about that later, but I don't know who perpetrated it. At the time when we military were passing through there, I did not hear anything of that sort. Later I did hear and I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What did you hear later? Can you give us any details, anything you remember about what you heard?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a couple of years later, that I learned that some civilians were found dead or killed some years before, but I don't know how they were killed nor who killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear anything about the village of Nadin being burnt or a large part of it was set fire in the evening of the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because we were at Benkovac by that time. The military and the TO were in Benkovac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one final topic -- actually, I'm surprised even myself with my ability to speed things up. You mentioned that another -- a nurse by the name of Zorana Banic is serving a prison sentence in Croatia and you explained how you think that she has been unjustly convicted. You yourself were also convicted in absentia by Croatian courts for crimes that they say were committed in Skabrnja in the events that we've been talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zorana Banic was not in Skabrnja at all. I was in Skabrnja, but I'm not a criminal. I helped people. And I'm glad that I had this opportunity before this Court to say that. And of course, I am sorry for a woman who hasn't hurt a fly and who was not in Skabrnja. Zorana does not know me. I know her and her family, and I know that she wasn't in Skabrnja, and now she's in Croatian prison and she has been unjustly convicted and sentenced to six years. I was invited through the Interpol and testified at the palace of justice in Belgrade. I heeded the summons and I testified there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Witness, that the Prosecutor asked you a couple of questions about what happened as you said on the 30th of September, 1991, in the vicinity of Nadin when you entered a minefield? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the reason for that action on the part of the JNA? What was the intended goal? Why did the JNA set out towards Nadin?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because from Nadinska Glava, Benkovac was shelled a couple of days before that, and the roads between Benkovac and Biljane Gornje and Benkovac and Biljane Donje was unpassable. Neither the military nor civilians, the people tending their fields could not pass that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When was that situation like that, when you say that there was shelling? How long before the 30th of September? When did it begin?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it happened from time to time, then two days would go by, then again, and so on. So Biljane Gornje were attacked that way with shells, and from that elevation, you would go to the airport, but you couldn't pass that way because everything was mined up until the road, up to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that from Nadin, they shot from Nadin, what did they use? What weapons? What happened at Biljane and the road? How was this targeted?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can use weapons, rifles, machine-guns, mortars, targeting Benkovac and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did -- were these mortars active? How long were they used? I don't think you understand my question. If you look at the 30th of September, when did the mortars go into action? Ten, 15 days, a month prior to that? Do you understand what I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it went on for about a month. As soon as somebody appeared, there would be shooting. So you were never sure of a free passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why these people at Nadinska Kosa armed themselves? Who armed them?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the HDZ armed them. The party that came into power. And broke up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? You say the HDZ armed them. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because everybody in my village was armed by the HDZ. They received weapons from the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the targeting from Nadin and Nadinska Kosa made it impossible for the JNA to move around. What consequences did this have on the JNA? The consequences of those actions?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, the JNA had its materiel at the airport. They couldn't pull it out. They couldn't have -- their food couldn't arrive, and people were left without a means of livelihood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I know when you said that there was targeting at Zemunik but how do you know that the JNA lacked food? How could you have known that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it couldn't have had any food because the road was blocked and food supplies couldn't reach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If the main road was blocked, wasn't there any other route to approach Zemunik?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the main road and the only road from Smiljcici, Tromilje, Zemunik Donji via Biljane. And later on you had to pass through some woods towards Smokovic, a Serbian village, behind the airport. And what was targeted was Suhovar [phoen] where you could lose your life every day and that's where most people were killed, on that section of the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, is this what you're saying, that before the 30th of September, 1991, the JNA didn't use the road taking it through the fields, the by-road but used that later on?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the reason for the JNA to advance towards Nadin? You were with the medical corps. What were you told?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that there was a blockade of the Ravni Kotari road leading to the Ravni Kotari villages and that there was a blockade towards the airport and Biljane, Benkovac-Biljane Donje, that road, and the Serbian part of Zemunik Gornji, were inaccessible by the road. You had to go through the woods and the upper part through Biljane Gornje, Kasic and Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember my learned friend of the Prosecution asking you, and I think that Their Honours asked you that question as well, whether the JNA moved towards Nadin first on that date, the 30th of September, 1991? I'm sure you will remember that question.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA advanced towards Nadin, what did it represent in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the army, the Yugoslav People's Army, in fact, an army which had its normal tasks and assignments and among which it said that it had to defend the sovereignty of its state, of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to you, what were the people in Nadin and at Nadinska Kosa who used mortars and artillery weapons to fire, what were they?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who were they fighting against?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the existing state at that time, Yugoslavia, which was the country they inhabited too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when my learned friend of the Prosecution asked you a question linked to the post-mortem report?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you gave us a -- told us about your CV you said that you had completed secondary administrative school, that you are an administrative worker in fact?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did complete that school, but I didn't work as an administrative worker. I worked in a company called Jugoplastika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any medical schools?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the civilian protection of the Jugoplastika firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from the courses that you mentioned having attended, did -- have you got any official training in the field of medicine?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just first aid. Otherwise not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say you were in the civilian protection service and that you worked with first aid, is that all you -- all the knowledge you have in the field of medicine, just your first aid course and first aid training; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned the events in Skabrnja of the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, you were asked who took part in that operation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in response to a question you explained many times that you were in Biljane Donje and in Trpolje [as interpreted] and you left after the shooting had started?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us once again how did it come about that from Trljuge as a member of the medical corps in a TO unit from Benkovac, you happened to go to the hamlet of Ambar? Who called you to go there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence Lakic called me to go there and the command from Skabrnja, where a soldier was killed, because we were on a radio connection, a radio line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you set out together with the JNA unit, in the morning, and that you arrived in Trljuge, when you say "we arrived in Trljuge," who do you mean, who is the "we"?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The medical corps arrived in Trljuge. It's a hamlet in Biljane Donje. Trljuge is a hamlet in Biljane Donje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you whether the JNA and the TO had taken part in any fighting? Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what your answer was? Your answer was that you -- or, rather, that the TO units -- or, rather, that the TO on that day, the 18th and 19th of November, were under JNA command?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You as a member of the TO's medical corps, come under the command of the JNA as well?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you about how you knew that the civilians with the soldiers were together in the houses by the road? Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Prosecutor also asked you how come you knew that the civilians were in the houses together with people who were armed?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how you come to claim that it was the civilians and the people who shot at you were in the same cellars in the same houses if you didn't enter those houses and cellars?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in front of the windows of the cellar, as far as I was able to see, there were sandbags, which were protection for the soldiers, and because there was shooting coming from the cellars and the civilians who left those cellars, or that cellar, and made their way out were taken by us to I think something that was called Krncetina, that particular district. But there was shooting coming from the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in connection with those civilians that emerged from the cellar, the ones you saw, can you tell us what the attitude of the JNA soldiers was towards them. At that point in time when they appeared and there was general shooting in the village, what did the JNA soldiers do?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA soldiers led them towards Krncetina or pointed them in that direction so that the people could take safety there and save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember Judge Moloto asking you at one point about whether or not you had seen any people who were wounded, killed and so on, and these questions were linked to the fatalities and the casualties?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as a nurse, on the spot, who did you receive information from? Who told you where there was somebody who needed first aid and because they were wounded or injured? Who gave that you information?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the soldiers gave you that information, which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence within its composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When there were civilians who were wounded and injured, who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what your attitude was and the attitude of the people who took in those civilians and wounded civilians, so both civilians who were uninjured and those who were. What was their attitude towards those civilians?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see -- or, rather, my team helped the people, administered first aid, dressed their wounds. Now, we had nothing to do with the dead people, those who had been killed. That -- they were dealt with later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was another question from the Prosecutor asking you whether you just moved along the road and you didn't happen to venture away from the road?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether, in Skabrnja, in Skabrnja itself, Skabrnja proper, there were any areas that had been mined?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skabrnja was mined throughout, from Ambar through the length of the road towards Biljane Gornje, Razovljeva Glava and linked to Nadin and Nadinska Glava towards Rastevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the whole area was mined, how did you happen to know that? Did you know that at the time when the fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first mines that I saw a were dismantled at the entrance to Skabrnja, the anti-tank mines. And in Nadin, I knew about the mines in Nadin before that because I was on the minefield pulling out two wounded soldiers from a tank, which had come across anti-tank mines, and I stepped onto the minefield, they were trip mines, but luckily I didn't step on any one and they were dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th -- 18th and 19th of November, 1991, when you arrived at Nadinska Kosa, were there any mines? Was anybody injured? Or not?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a minefield that had been laid, and we came across the anti-tank mines and some of the soldiers were killed. Were wounded, sorry, soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Anti-personnel mines, not anti-tank mines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The time has elapsed. How much longer are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've almost reached the end, just perhaps one more question, Your Honour. Might I just take a moment to consult my notes? My last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you on several occasions, several times, whether you testified here -- whether you changed the facts, distorted the facts, hid the facts, in order to justify something. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you indeed tell us what you saw and what you know?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I knew, the truth as I knew it, what I did not know I could not answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That completes my examination of this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, please, following general question. How come that Mr. Zoran Lakic asked you to be part of that operation?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it is not Dragan Lakic, it is Zoran Lakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I said Zoran, Zoran Lakic.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I was in the civilian protection of Jugoplastika, a member of the Territorial Defence, of course every inhabitant of the country, well, they asked me to be a member of the civilian defence. I received an invitation to come, and I responded to the call-up, and if you didn't respond that would entail certain steps to be taken against you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And what was the chain of command above you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. How do you mean above me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
